explain.prompt: For each feature, give in one line the economic reason a trader might care about it. Then, using the screening table of the test code (correlation with the crack change in 2017–18 and in 2019): which features would you keep and why? Finally, explain why every market feature is shifted by one day, and why `month` is not.
rubric: Origin = morning of day t, before day t's settlement: only settlements up to t−1 are known, so every feature built from prices is shifted by one day (a rolling window that includes t would use the answer).

change_lag1: persistence or reversal of yesterday's move; mean_change_20: recent drift; vol_change_20: recent risk regime; gap_to_mean_60: how stretched the crack is (mean reversion of margins); corr_gasoil_60: strength of the transatlantic diesel link; month / heating_season: seasonal demand.
Calendar variables are known in advance (the date of tomorrow is not news), so they need no shift.

Screening: change_lag1 (≈ −0.16 then −0.22) and gap_to_mean_60 (≈ −0.07 then −0.11) have a stable sign and an economic reason (reversal of daily noise, mean reversion of the crack); vol_change_20, corr_gasoil_60 and heating_season change sign or are ≈ 0 — not supported.
A feature is kept for an economic reason AND a stable relationship, not for its in-sample correlation alone; with many candidates, some will look good by chance.
Rolling windows need gap-free inputs: with holiday NaNs, a 20-day window returns NaN for 20 days after every holiday — that is why the treated prices are used.
